This is CF 737-18 or Criminal Appeal 2019-12 in the matter of People of Guam versus Joshua Brandon Perez. In this matter, Mr. Perez was indicted on December 10, 2018 on two charges. The first charge was possession with intent to deliver an amphetamine-based substance and the second charge was possession of a controlled substance, which is an amphetamine-based substance. Both charges were accompanied by a special allegation, a notice, commission of a felony while on felony release. We raised three issues before the court this morning. First of the three issues is that the executed waiver by Mr. Perez was invalid as it was not voluntary, knowing and intelligent. The second issue is insufficiency of the evidence as there was no evidence presented to show that methamphetamine was an amphetamine-based substance. And the third issue is that Perez's five-year sentence for the special allegation was not within the statutory limit. On the first issue, United States Supreme Court in Apprendi versus New Jersey determined that facts that support a sentencing enhancement must be submitted to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court made clear that there's no difference between elements of a crime charged or sentencing factors. If the fact increases the maximum penalty, then both must be submitted to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court later decided in Blakely versus Washington that this right to have a jury trial can be waived. This court has adopted the standard put forth by the United States Supreme Court in Blakely versus Washington, and has found and created a test in several cases to determine when a waiver is valid. Specifically, this court, and I think most recently in People versus Chong, 2019 Guam 30, this court made clear that if a defendant either stipulates to a fact on felony release, or if a defendant stipulates to a fact on felony release and makes a conscious objective to have that fact not go before the jury, then he has validly waived his apprendee rights. And in this matter, we argue that Mr. Perez did not validly waive his apprendee rights, and for several reasons. First, there was no initial stipulation to a fact on felony release. And we do argue that it was not his conscious objective to expose himself to a greater punishment that was authorized by the jury's verdict. Mr. Perez, again.
